lead: Both people are afraid of getting the short end, and both may end up with it.
when: When two people or two teams could cooperate but keep guarding against each other out of fear of free riders or of losing out by going first, use it to examine the rules underneath.
body:
Two people are working on something together. Clearly, cooperating would be better for both, yet each can't help thinking: "If they do their part, I can slack a bit and come out ahead. If they don't, I'm certainly not going to work for nothing." So both choose not to cooperate, and the work turns out worse. That's the tension the prisoner's dilemma is meant to show us.

The prisoner's dilemma is a classic model in game theory: in the standard one-shot, two-player game, not cooperating is each player's dominant strategy, yet the payoff to each when both don't cooperate is lower than when both cooperate.

In the classic story, two suspects are questioned separately. As the puzzle is set up, no matter what the other person chooses, confessing gets you a somewhat lighter punishment. But if both confess, both are punished more heavily than if both had stayed silent. This is a hypothetical structure of choices, not a description of how real criminal cases work.

Its most useful reminder is that when cooperation fails, it isn't always because someone has "bad character." It may be that the rules make not cooperating look like the better deal. To improve the outcome, besides showing good faith, look for ways to make contributions visible and commitments enforceable, so neither side has to protect itself by guessing.

To read the four-box grid, let the rows be your choices and the columns the other person's, each ordered "cooperate, don't cooperate." Look at both people's payoffs in each box. Then compare your two options down the same column, and the other person's two options along the same row. That's how you see why individual choices can lead both sides to a worse result.
example:
Suppose you and a classmate agree to each organize half of the review notes and then share them. To make the relationships clear, we'll use hypothetical "net payoff scores": the help the notes give you minus the effort of organizing them. Higher is better, and these aren't real measurements. If both of you do your part, you each get 3. If you don't and your classmate does, you get 5 and they get 0. The reverse gives you 0 and them 5. If neither of you does it, you each get 1.

From your side: if your classmate does their part, skipping yours moves you from 3 to 5. If they don't, skipping yours moves you from 0 to 1. Your classmate makes the same comparison, so neither of you does it and you each get 1, worse than the 3 each you'd get by cooperating. That's the dilemma: the choice that looks better to each person on their own doesn't leave the two of you better off together.

In real life, you can change how you cooperate: each hand in a small portion first and continue once the quality checks out, and spell out each person's tasks and deadlines so contributions can be verified. That changes the conditions for cooperation, rather than just asking the other person to "trust me."
extra:
Two neighboring teams both need to maintain a shared document. Maintaining it takes time, while just reading the other team's updates is easy. If both try to free-ride, the document gets more and more outdated until it's useless to everyone. Whether this is a strict prisoner's dilemma depends on how each side really weighs the time against the value of the information, but it's a reminder to ask "who bears the cost, and who gets the benefit?"

You could try rotating updates, defining what each team maintains, recording contributions, and having both sides flag gaps promptly. The key is to make the effort and the payoff of cooperating line up more easily, rather than repeatedly blaming the other side for not taking the initiative.
steps: Write down each side's two choices, list the four combinations, and see who each outcome favors.
Check why not cooperating is tempting: is it easy to free-ride, are commitments impossible to verify, or is there a fear of not being paid back?
Start with one small, verifiable round of cooperation with clear deliverables, feedback, and a way out, then decide whether to continue.
caution: Not every bumpy collaboration is a prisoner's dilemma. The classic one-shot model requires that not cooperating is better for you no matter what the other side does, yet both not cooperating is worse for both than both cooperating. Real-life payoffs, relationships, and motives may not fit that setup. Repeated cooperation, public information, or rule changes may change the outcome, but success isn't guaranteed. Understanding the dilemma doesn't mean always giving in; protecting your boundaries and knowing when to walk away matter just as much.
exercise: Find something where you and someone else are both waiting for the other to go first. Draw four boxes and fill in the outcomes for "we both do it," "only I do it," "only they do it," and "neither of us does it." Then write down one small arrangement that would lower the risk of going first.
brief: Two-sided choices and a shared loss: two stick figures on separate sides each decide whether to put a gear into a shared machine or keep it on their own side. A faint small scene above shows a bridge connected after cooperation; the main scene below shows both taking their gears back, the bridge broken, and both stuck. No text; a narrative scene rather than a matrix.
diagramCaption: Rows and columns are both ordered cooperate, don't cooperate. In each box, the navy dots on top show your net payoff and the brick-red dots below show the other person's; the four boxes are 3 and 3, 0 and 5, 5 and 0, and 1 and 1, as a hypothetical example only.
